t: and he does not receive lashes for this prohibition since he did no act. And one is not flogged for a transgression unless it involves an act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2).
the rejoicing mentioned regarding the festivals etc.. See Hilchot Yom Tov 6:17, that included in this rejoicing is that he rejoice with the members of his family, each in the manner that suits him.

that he bring peace offerings in addition to the chagigah peace offerings. And rejoice by eating their meat (see below 2:10). This obligation applies throughout all the days of the festival (Hilchot Yom Tov there; and see below, halacha 4).
and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and eat there and rejoice. From this it follows that rejoicing is accomplished by eating the meat of peace offerings.
it has no measure by Torah law. There is no fixed price for the offering that must be brought, and he may bring it at any price he wishes.
a silver ma'ah. Silver weighing sixteen barleycorns (Hilchot Eruvin 1:12).
and it is a mitzvah to bring according to one's wealth. To add to the price of the burnt offering and the peace offerings according to his ability.
if he had the offerings of appearance etc.. He should bring up, for the sake of offering the burnt offering of appearance, the animals themselves or silver coins with which to buy them.
he should not bring their value. Objects worth the value of the offering.
a decree lest he not find anyone to sell. The value in silver, and will not be able to buy the offerings.
or lest the coins be found to be debased. That the coins that are given him will be inferior, and he will not be able to buy a proper animal with them.

one who did not bring on the first festival day his burnt offering of appearance and his chagigah peace offerings etc.. These offerings should initially be brought on the first day (above, halacha 1, below, halacha 5) and the other days are make-up days for the first, whereas the peace offerings of rejoicing are obligatory on all the days of the festival (Rivash, and see below 2:5).

and about him it is said: 'I have gathered those grieving from the appointed time'. Sorrow and brokenness will come upon those who are late for the festivals (based on Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 28a).
the festival passed and he did not celebrate. He did not bring the offerings.
he is not liable for it. He is not obligated to bring it after the festival (see Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 1:7).
what is crooked cannot be made straight. For what has passed and he did not bring is a transgression that has no remedy.
and the last festival day, which is Shemini Atzeret. Shemini Atzeret.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in explaining the verses.

that the festival of Shavuot is like the festival of Passover for make-up. Just as on Passover they offer during the seven days of the festival, so too on Shavuot they offer on the first day and the six days after it (though they are weekdays).

they do not override Shabbat. When the first festival day falls on Shabbat (or one who did not offer them at the beginning of the festival and wishes to offer them on Shabbat), they offer them after Shabbat.
nor impurity. They may not be offered in impurity, even when most of the congregation or the priests are impure.
because they have no fixed time like the community offerings. Community offerings, since their time is fixed, override Shabbat and impurity (Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash 4:9).
as we have explained. That he may complete the offering on the other days (above, halacha 4).
vows and freewill offerings. Individual offerings that a person brings as a vow or a freewill offering.
he leans on them. In individual offerings the owner must lean on the head of the offering before its slaughter (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 3:6).
as he does on other days. Ibid., halacha 13.
even though leaning is not indispensable, as we explained in Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot. Ibid., halacha 12.

they did not decree against it because of shevut. By rabbinic law it is forbidden to lean on an animal (Hilchot Shabbat 21:9). But for the sake of offering the sacrifice the Sages did not forbid leaning.
heirs are obligated to bring it. The heirs bring the offerings of the one they inherit from (see also Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:13).
those who eat from many. Many members of the household who eat at his table.

he may increase the chagigah peace offerings and lessen the burnt offerings of appearance. That he may bring several burnt offerings for his appearance and several peace offerings for his chagigah (see below 2:6-7).
from appearance. Going up to the Temple courtyard and bringing a burnt offering on the festival (above 1:1).
and the lame. One with a defect in his legs that causes him to limp.
and the delicate and very frail who cannot go up on their feet. They cannot go up to the Temple courtyard themselves.
a deaf person, even though he speaks. Unlike the deaf person usually spoken of in halacha, who neither hears nor speaks (Hilchot Ishut 2:26).
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not evident whether he is male or female. [Note: in the Commentary to the Mishnah Rambam vocalizes this word 'tumtum'.]
and an androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.
who is half slave and half free. One who had two partner owners and one of them freed him, or whose owner freed half of him (see Hilchot Avadim 7:4).
and a positive commandment from which women are exempt. Such as positive commandments that are time-bound, from which women are exempt (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3).

for it says: when all Israel comes. This verse and the verses later in the halacha were said regarding the mitzvah of Hakhel, and from what is said in them regarding appearance, they derived (Babylonian Talmud Chagigah 3a).
to exclude one who does not hear completely. A deaf person, even in one ear.
to exclude one who does not speak, for the whole mitzvah is to teach. And one who cannot speak cannot teach and therefore is exempt (see also Hilchot Talmud Torah 1:1).
and we have already explained in Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash. Chapter 3.
and likewise the uncircumcised is repulsive like the impure. And cannot bring an offering (see below, halacha 4).
one who refines copper at its mine. A copper miner.
and the tanners. Leather workers.
who are repulsive because of their work. A foul odor emanates from them (see Hilchot Ishut 25:11).
they purify their bodies and clothing. They clean themselves and their clothes and remove from them any foul odor.
a minor who can hold his father's hand and go up. And does not need to be carried.
even though he is fit for healing. And there would have been room to think that he should be trained so that he will go up after he is healed.
as we have explained. Above, halacha 1.
in the chagigah. Bringing a peace offering when he arrives at the Temple courtyard on the festival (above 1:1).
and all are obligated in rejoicing. Even those exempt from appearance and chagigah, such as women and slaves, are obligated to eat the meat of the peace offerings of rejoicing like men.
because they are not subject to obligation. For they lack understanding (Hilchot Ishut 3:17).
as we have explained in Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash. That an impure person is not fit to enter the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash chapter 3).
and in Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot. That an uncircumcised or impure person may not eat of the holy offerings (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 10:9).

for all the days of the festival are make-up days for the first. The possibility of offering on the other days is as a supplement for offerings not brought on the first day, and one who was exempt on the first day is exempt from offering on the other days.
as we have explained. Above 1:4.

and likewise if he became impure on the nights of the first festival day. So that at the beginning of the time of obligation, which is on the morning of the first festival day (since offerings may be brought only by day), he was impure.
even though he became pure the next day. The next evening, after he immersed and nightfall came.
but if he became impure on the first day, he is obligated. Since he became impure on the first day after he was obligated in the offerings, he is obligated to complete them when he becomes pure.
is only at the main part of the festival. The first time he arrives.
for appearance has no measure. And he may bring as many burnt offerings as he wishes.

he no longer returns and brings the rest. Unlike the burnt offering of appearance, which he may bring throughout all the days of the festival (above, halacha 6), the chagigah peace offerings must be offered only on the first day or in its make-up days.
for he left them over. He showed that he intends to leave them and offer them tomorrow.
the day pressed him. The day ended before he managed to offer them.
he offers the rest tomorrow. Since he did not manage to offer them on the first day, the second day is considered a make-up for the first day.

the burnt offering of appearance comes only from non-sacred property, like the other offerings that a person is obligated to bring. Every offering that a person is obligated to bring must be bought with non-sacred money or be a non-sacred animal he owns, and he cannot bring it from an animal or money that is already sacred (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 16:15).

chagigah peace offerings come from second-tithe money mixed with non-sacred money etc.. Money onto which second tithe was transferred must be brought up to Jerusalem, where food is bought with it and eaten in purity. He may buy an animal with it for a peace offering (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 7:12), but he cannot bring with it a peace offering he is already obligated to bring (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot there). However, when he buys the chagigah animal with second-tithe money and non-sacred money together, he fulfills the chagigah obligation with the part purchased with non-sacred money.

and a person fulfills the obligation of chagigah peace offerings with animal tithe. Although animal tithe is not non-sacred, one fulfills the chagigah obligation with it (and the commentators found the reason for this difficult; see Lechem Mishneh and Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
and they do not bring it on a festival. The animal tithe that is offered as a chagigah.

a decree lest he tithe on a festival. When tithing animals, the tenth animal is marked with paint, and out of concern that they might paint, it is forbidden to tithe on Shabbat and a festival (Hilchot Shabbat 23:14).
in vows and freewill offerings. Peace offerings that they undertook to bring as a vow or a freewill offering.
in a sin offering, a guilt offering, and a firstborn. Whose meat is eaten by the priests.
and in the breast and the thigh. Which are given to the priests from the peace offerings.
for this mitzvah is to rejoice by eating meat before the Lord. And therefore one can fulfill the obligation of rejoicing before the Lord by eating the meat of any offering.
we have already explained in the laws of Passover offerings. Hilchot Korban Pesach 10:13.
that the chagigah of the fourteenth is optional. The peace offerings that one offers on the fourteenth of Nisan with the Passover offering, there is no obligation to offer.

therefore a person does not fulfill the obligation of chagigah with it. For one fulfills the chagigah obligation only with non-sacred property (but if the chagigah of the fourteenth were obligatory, it could also exempt him from the obligation of the chagigah of the fifteenth; Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
but he fulfills the obligation of rejoicing with it. For one may fulfill the obligation of rejoicing also with offerings slaughtered before the festival (below, halacha 11).
on the fourteenth day. Of Nisan, Passover eve.

because of the chametz in it. The thanksgiving offering and its bread are eaten on the day of offering and the night after, and with the thanksgiving offering they would bring loaves, some of which are leavened. Since on Passover eve from midday chametz is forbidden to eat, if he slaughters a thanksgiving offering on Passover eve he shortens the time fit for eating the thanksgiving offering's loaves and brings forward the time they become disqualified.
for one does not bring sacred things to a disqualifying situation. One does not bring sacred things into a situation that might cause them to be disqualified.

and if he brought it, he fulfills the obligation of rejoicing with it. When he slaughters a thanksgiving offering on Passover eve he eats it on the night of the festival and fulfills the obligation of rejoicing with it then (for unlike the other festivals, on which the mitzvah of rejoicing does not apply on the night of the festival, on Passover there is an obligation already on the night of the festival; Chazon Ish).
as we have explained. That he fulfills the obligation of rejoicing by eating the meat of offerings slaughtered on the eve of a festival (above, halacha 10).

he is obligated to bring a thanksgiving offering etc.. When he said 'I take upon myself a thanksgiving offering' he became obligated to bring it, and his condition that he stated afterward is void (for a similar law see Hilchot Nezirut 8:14).
according to his wealth. According to his financial ability.

'Their sacrifices shall be like the bread of mourners; all who eat of it shall be defiled, for their bread is for their own appetite'. The meat they eat will be like the food of mourners, which defiles the one who eats it, because they eat for themselves and do not share with the poor. This is not the joy of a mitzvah but the joy of the belly (Hilchot Yom Tov 6:18, and see Hilchot Megillah 2:17).
a portion. In the spoils when conquering the cities in the land (Hilchot Shemitah ve-Yovel 13:10).
an inheritance. He does not receive land in the inheritance of the Land.
and he has no gifts of meat. Like the priests, who receive from the meat of non-sacred animals (Hilchot Bikkurim 9:1) and from the meat of the offerings.
their tithe. The first tithe given to them from the produce of the ground.
at the end of every Sabbatical cycle. In the eighth year.
when they go up for the festival. On the festival of Sukkot (below, halacha 3).
in the true religion. In faith in the Creator.
one exempt from appearance. Above 2:1.

and the uncircumcised. He is exempt from appearance because he is repulsive and cannot bring an offering, but he may enter the Temple Mount and the Women's Courtyard, and therefore is obligated in Hakhel (Rivash).
the impure is exempt from the mitzvah of Hakhel... is not fit to enter. He is forbidden to enter the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at ha-Mikdash 3:1).
and in the Women's Courtyard. Which was to the east of the Temple courtyard (Hilchot Beit ha-Bechirah 5:7).

and the synagogue attendant takes a Torah scroll and gives it to the head of the synagogue, and the head of the synagogue gives it to the deputy. They would pass the scroll from person to person to show the importance of the king (similar to Hilchot Avodat Yom ha-Kippurim 3:10). The synagogue attendant is the sexton of the synagogue, and the head of the synagogue is the synagogue administrator. The deputy is the deputy of the priests, the second to the high priest.
and the king receives it standing, and if he wishes, sitting. After receiving the scroll standing he may, if he wishes, sit (Mount Moriah).
and he opens and blesses the way every reader of the Torah in the synagogue blesses. 'Who has chosen us' (Hilchot Tefillah 12:5).
and rolls. Closes the Torah scroll.
and blesses after it as is done in synagogues. 'Who has given us the Torah of truth' (ibid.).
and adds seven blessings. Similar to the blessings the high priest adds after reading from the Torah scroll on Yom Kippur (Hilchot Avodat Yom ha-Kippurim 3:11).
these are three blessings in their usual form. As we pray in the Amidah on festivals.
to the confused and converts who do not know etc.. Who do not understand the holy language, and nevertheless they must prepare their hearts and listen.
even great Sages who know the entire Torah are obligated to listen. For a similar law see Hilchot Chametz u-Matzah 7:1.
Hakhel day. The first day of the intermediate days of the festival.
